lemma_proposals.statement: For every nonzero rational x such that 1+x and 1−x are rational squares, there exist coprime integers m,n with n>0, m≠0, m≠±n such that x=4mn(n²−m²)/(m²+n²)². For every such primitive pair, putting q=m²+n² and r=q/gcd(q,2), the reduced denominator of this value is r², r is odd and at least 5, every prime divisor of r is congruent to 1 modulo 4, and the reduced numerator is divisible by 24. These statements concern each neighbor individually and assert no mutual-edge condition.
assumptions: A common neighbor of −1 and 1 means a nonzero rational x for which 1+x and 1−x are rational squares.
The integers m,n in the parametrization are coprime and n>0.
quantifiers: For every nonzero rational common neighbor x, there exists a primitive pair m,n with n>0 and m≠0, m≠±n that gives the stated parametrization.
For every primitive pair m,n with n>0 and m≠0, m≠±n, the denominator, prime-divisor, and numerator conclusions hold.
lemma_proposals.proof:
Choose rational u,v with u²=1+x and v²=1−x. Then u²+v²=2. Since x≠0, u≠1, so the line through (1,1) and (u,v) has finite rational slope t=(v−1)/(u−1). Its second intersection with U²+V²=2 has coordinates U=(t²−2t−1)/(t²+1), V=(1−2t−t²)/(t²+1). Therefore x=U²−1=4t(1−t²)/(1+t²)². Write t=m/n in lowest terms, n>0. The nonzero condition on x implies m≠0 and m≠±n. With q=m²+n², we have x=N/q², where N=4mn(n²−m²).

For any odd prime p dividing q, p divides neither m nor n. If p also divided n²−m², then n²≡m² and n²≡−m² modulo p, so p divides 2m², a contradiction. Thus no odd prime divisor of q cancels against N. If q is odd, m,n have opposite parity and N is divisible by 8; q² has no factor 2 to cancel. If q is even, coprimality makes m,n odd, q≡2 mod 8, and 8 divides n²−m². Thus v₂(N)≥5 while v₂(q²)=2, so exactly a factor 4 cancels at 2. These cases give the reduced denominator r² with r=q/gcd(q,2), which is odd. For every odd prime p dividing r, m²≡−n² modulo p and n is nonzero modulo p; hence −1 is a quadratic residue modulo p and p≡1 mod 4. Also r≥5: for odd q, a sum of two nonzero squares cannot be 1 or 3; for even q, q≡2 mod 8, and r=1 would force q=2 and m=±n, which is excluded.

The reduced numerator is divisible by 8: this follows from mn even when q is odd, and from 8∣(n²−m²) followed by cancellation of only 4 when q is even. For divisibility by 3, either 3 divides mn or m,n are both nonzero modulo 3 and their squares agree, giving 3∣(n²−m²). In either case q is not divisible by 3: if m²+n²≡0 modulo 3, both m and n must be divisible by 3, contrary to coprimality. Thus reducing the fraction does not remove a factor of 3 from the numerator. The reduced numerator is consequently divisible by both 8 and 3, hence by 24.

lemma_proposals.statement: For every finite set S of primes, there are infinitely many distinct sets {−1,1,x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄} of distinct nonzero rationals with 0<xᵢ<1 such that all pairwise product-plus-one values involving either anchor are rational squares, and each xᵢxⱼ+1 for i<j is a square in Qₚ for every p∈S. No claim is made that these six mutual values are rational squares.
assumptions: S is any finite set of primes, possibly empty.
A square in Qₚ means a square in the p-adic field Qₚ.
quantifiers: For every finite set S of primes.
There exist infinitely many distinct six-element sets satisfying the specified rational and p-adic square conditions.
lemma_proposals.proof:
Let P be the product of the primes in S, with P=1 if S is empty. For positive integers k put L=1+kP and tᵢ=iP/L for i=1,2,3,4. As k grows, all tᵢ tend to zero, and they are strictly increasing in i. Define F(t)=4t(1−t²)/(1+t²)² and xᵢ=F(tᵢ). Since F′(0)=4, there is an interval (0,ε) on which F is strictly increasing and 0<F(t)<1. For all sufficiently large k, the tᵢ lie in this interval, so the xᵢ are distinct and in (0,1). As k increases, t₁ and hence x₁ strictly decrease; x₁ is the least of the four xᵢ, so these k yield infinitely many distinct sets.

Direct expansion gives 1+F(t)=((t²−2t−1)/(1+t²))² and 1−F(t)=((1−2t−t²)/(1+t²))². Thus each xᵢ has rational-square edges to both anchors; the anchor edge has value (−1)(1)+1=0, also a rational square.

Fix p∈S. Then p∣P and L≡1 modulo p, so vₚ(tᵢ)≥1. The factors 1±tᵢ² are p-adic units. The formula for F implies vₚ(xᵢ)≥1 for odd p, and v₂(xᵢ)=2+v₂(tᵢ)≥3 when p=2. Therefore, for y=xᵢxⱼ, vₚ(y)≥1 for odd p and v₂(y)≥3 for p=2.

For odd p, 1+y has a square root in Zₚ: start with r₁=1, a root modulo p of Z²−(1+y). If r_h²≡1+y modulo p^h, write 1+y−r_h²=p^h d. Choose c modulo p satisfying 2r_hc≡d modulo p; this is possible because r_h is a unit and p is odd. Then r_{h+1}=r_h+cp^h satisfies r_{h+1}²≡1+y modulo p^{h+1}. The compatible approximations converge in Zₚ to a square root.

For p=2, 1+y≡1 modulo 8, so r₃=1 is a square root modulo 8. Given an odd r_h with r_h²≡1+y modulo 2^h for h≥3, replacing it by r_h+2^{h−1} changes its square by 2^h r_h+2^{2h−2}, which is congruent to 2^h modulo 2^{h+1}. Thus either r_h or r_h+2^{h−1} has square congruent to 1+y modulo 2^{h+1}. Choose that value as r_{h+1}. These choices converge 2-adically because successive changes have valuations tending to infinity; their limit squares to 1+y. Applying the appropriate lifting argument to each y proves all the asserted local-square conditions. This establishes only the finite-local statement, not rational square roots for the six mutual values.
